title: Stalactites vs stalagmites: ceiling or floor?

sources.name: National Park Service — Gap Cave and protecting cave formations
USGS — An Unseen World Beneath Our Feet

practice: Explore more of the natural world in Science Quiz.

sections.html:
Stalactites hang from a cave ceiling; stalagmites grow upwards from the floor. When a matching pair joins, it forms a column.

Look at where the formation is attached, rather than guessing from its shape. The National Park Service’s cave guide shows both. For another natural-world puzzle, try the Science Quiz.
sections.title: What is the difference?

sections.html:
The c in stalactite can remind you of the ceiling. The g in stalagmite points you towards the ground.

That is a spelling trick, not the origin of the words. Picture a cave with one shape hanging down and another reaching up: two similar names, opposite starting points.
sections.title: C for ceiling, G for ground

sections.html:
In many limestone caves, water carries dissolved calcium carbonate. As it loses carbon dioxide, some mineral can come out of the water as solid calcite.

Tiny deposits build up over many drips, on the ceiling or underneath on the floor. A thin, hollow stalactite is called a soda straw. Apparently caves have their own drinks accessories.
sections.title: How can dripping water build rock?

sections.html:
Growth depends on conditions such as water supply and chemistry, so length alone cannot tell you a reliable age.

On a visit, admire formations from the permitted route. For another small natural-world puzzle, discover what the delay between lightning and thunder can tell you.
